issues.legal_issue: Christians governed by the applicable customary personal law cannot claim a right to partition their living father's property, and succession legislation does not determine rights arising from his lifetime disposition.
material_facts: The father and his sons were Christians governed by the customary personal law applicable in the territory.
The father was alive when he executed the instrument on which the sons based their claim to the property.
The sons claimed under a lifetime transfer, not by succession following an intestate death.
issues.conclusion: The customary Hindu law applicable to the parties governed their rights; under that law the sons could not demand partition of their father's property during his lifetime. The Hindu Succession Act did not govern the Christian parties and, in any event, concerns devolution on intestacy rather than the lifetime transfer at issue.
issues.legal_principle: The 1817 Regulation made the French Code applicable while preserving the customs governing Indians' personal law; the 1880 Regulation addressed the application of civil procedure and civil-status rules. Christians in the relevant territory remained governed in other personal-law matters by customary Hindu law. Under that customary law, sons could not demand partition of their father's property during his lifetime. Section 2(1)(c) of the Hindu Succession Act excludes Christians from the Act's application, and the Act governs devolution on intestacy rather than lifetime dispositions. No earlier cases are relied on for this determination.

predicates.civil_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to rights in property.
predicates.territory_applies_customary_personal_law: The territory applies customary personal law to Christians in matters of personal law relevant to the dispute.
predicates.parties_are_christians: The father and the children whose rights are claimed are Christians.
predicates.claim_arises_from_lifetime_disposition_b: The children base their property claim on a disposition made by their father while he was alive.

issues.definition: When a property dispute involves Christians subject to customary personal law and a claim based on their living father's disposition, the customary law governs and the sons cannot demand partition from him.

issues.legal_issue: An absolute owner cannot establish a transfer to non-owners merely by describing a lifetime allocation as a partition when the requirements for an effective gift or family settlement have not been pleaded or proved.
material_facts: The property had been allotted to the father in an earlier partition, and he was its absolute owner.
The father later executed an instrument described as a partition, allotting property to his sons, who did not already jointly own it with him.
The sons claimed title under that instrument.
The claimants did not plead or establish that the instrument complied with the formalities required for a gift or donation inter vivos.
issues.conclusion: The instrument could not operate as a partition between joint owners, and the claimants did not establish that it was an effective gift or family settlement. It therefore did not establish their claimed title.
issues.legal_principle: A partition is between persons who jointly own property. An absolute owner who intends to give property to others may do so by a legally effective gift, donation, will, or family settlement, as applicable, but the relevant formalities must be satisfied. The Court relied on Articles 931 and 1075–1077 of the French Code, including the requirement that donations inter vivos comply with prescribed formalities and that distributions by ascendants be made in accordance with the rules for donations or wills. No earlier cases are relied on for this determination.

rule.if: civil_property_title_dispute and transferor_was_absolute_owner and beneficiaries_had_no_existing_joint_ownership and instrument_purported_to_partition_property and gift_or_settlement_formalities_not_pleaded_or_proved

predicates.civil_property_title_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to title to property.
predicates.transferor_was_absolute_owner: The person who executed the instrument owned the property absolutely before making it.
predicates.beneficiaries_had_no_existing_joint_owne: The persons allocated property under the instrument did not already jointly own it with the transferor.
predicates.instrument_purported_to_partition_proper: The transferor used an instrument framed as a partition to allocate property to the beneficiaries.
predicates.gift_or_settlement_formalities_not_plead: The beneficiaries did not plead or establish that the instrument satisfied the formal requirements for an effective gift or family settlement.

issues.definition: If an absolute owner purports to partition property to persons who do not already jointly own it, but the requirements for an effective gift or family settlement are not pleaded or proved, the instrument does not establish their title.
